text_a: The Paycheck, Explained: Everyone remembers their first paycheck, and everyone remembers the shock: the number you were promised, then the number you got. It arrives on one of the least designed documents of adult life. Canva makes it make sense. The campaign launches with a Pay Stub Makeover: real first-timers hand over a confusing stub (with personal data removed) and watch it become a clear, friendly visual story, from 'what I earned' to 'where it went' to 'what's mine'. Free templates let employers add a personal welcome note, and let anyone redesign and save their own as a keepsake. The line of thought: design is how things make sense. It is not financial advice. It is clarity, made by Canva, for the moment work becomes real.
text_b: Payday, Designed: Your first paycheck is the moment work becomes real, and it arrives as a document built to be ignored. Canva takes on the most important, least designed page in working life. We show first-time earners squinting at lines like 'PAYG' and 'deductions' and feeling a bit lost on their proudest day. Then Canva gives teams a Payday Kit: a plain-language visual decoder that explains each line, a welcome-to-payday note from the team, and a keepsake worth keeping. Payroll providers still own the numbers; Canva owns how it feels. A student challenge redesigns the payslip with fictional data, and HR teams adopt the best versions as templates. First payday becomes an onboarding ritual that says: we made this clear because you matter.

text_a: Frame It: The First Paycheck Wall: Everyone frames the first dollar a business earns. No one frames the first paycheck. Canva makes it a ritual. Upload or recreate your first stub, and Canva masks every sensitive detail by default, then helps you turn it into a frame-ready keepsake. Add notes like the hours it took, who you treated, or what you learned. Print it, post it, or hang it at your desk. Creators share theirs first; a public 'Paycheck Wall' collects stories without ever showing amounts. Employers can gift a First Stub Frame kit at onboarding, bringing Canva into the team on day one. The message: you didn't just get paid, you became someone who works. Make it worth framing.
text_b: The Paper One: Direct deposit killed the paper paycheck. The first one used to be framed on a wall. Now it's a buzz on your phone, gone before you notice. Canva brings the ritual back. Employers, from cafés to retail chains, get a 'First Payday' pack: a card, a frame-ready poster and a social tile that celebrate what the new hire actually did, such as '62 hours, 410 coffees, 0 spills (nearly)', rather than what they earned. New hires can also make their own in seconds, hide the figure if they like, and print or frame it through partners. The tone is mock-official, treating a first paycheck like the historic document it feels like. The result is a new workplace ritual, thousands of shareable keepsakes and a reason for small businesses to open Canva on day one.

text_a: Luck, Sewn Back: Christian Dior, famously superstitious, hid a sprig of lily of the valley in the hem of his dresses for luck. We reverse the ritual: a garment's second life earns its own. Every piece mended by Dior's ateliers receives a 'lucky stitch' in muguet-white thread, hidden in the hem or worn proudly on a cuff, the owner's choice. Films follow the petites mains repairing a worn Bar jacket, a cracked Lady Dior strap, a grandmother's scarf. Pop-up Retouche salons open in Paris, Seoul and New York and, for one week, mend anything from any brand. Owners tell us why they kept it. Luxury stops promising newness and starts promising a longer story.
text_b: The Second Signature: Couture has always been the art of fitting and refitting, yet luxury hides the mend as if it were shame. Dior turns it into authorship. Every piece repaired in the ateliers returns with a second signature, the initials of the petite main who mended it and the date, stitched into the lining. Owners can choose an invisible mend or a visible one, but the maker is always named. The campaign introduces these hands through short portrait films, follows mended pieces and their owners, and culminates in a Galerie Dior exhibition of objects whose value grew because they were repaired. The message is simple and unmistakably Dior: a piece is never finished, only passed to the next pair of hands.

text_a: On Me: Most lonely people aren't short of contacts. They're short of an easy first move. 'We should catch up' dies because reaching out feels like asking. On Me removes the ask. Send someone a pre-paid invitation to a specific place and time: 'Coffee at Rosa's, Thursday 4pm. On me.' They tap to accept, and Mastercard's sonic logo plays as a small 'hello'. After the meeting, they receive their own On Me to pass to someone else, so one invitation can start a chain of reunions. It never says 'lonely' and never sends cash, only a reason to show up. Launch in one city with independent cafés and a single issuer partner, then tell the stories of the chains. Priceless, made practical.
text_b: The Covered Invite: Lonely people rarely lack company so much as the nerve to ask for it. Inviting feels like imposing, and accepting feels like a cost. The Covered Invite removes both. Any Mastercard holder can send a simple digital invite to a coffee, a meal or a class at a participating independent venue. The invite carries one line: 'It's covered. Just come.' Mastercard pays for the guest's first item, who doesn't need a Mastercard, and either side can say 'maybe later' with no awkwardness. Merchants fill quiet hours, and the brand shows what Priceless means in practice: money clears the way so the moment itself can be priceless. Themed waves such as new neighbours, old friends and the first week back can keep the platform running through the year.

'On Me' turns the invitation into a payment. Anyone can text an invite with a small single-use virtual Mastercard preloaded for one coffee, one ticket or one round, valid only at the named local venue and date. The guest pays nothing, so the yes costs nothing. Participating venues set up 'On Me' tables, and Mastercard seeds the first invitations through partners. Because the host chooses to pay, it stays a gesture between people, not charity. The film dwells on the moment before the yes: the thumb hovering, the excuse typed and deleted. Money can't buy company, but it can remove the reason to say no.

text_a: Priceless Regulars: For many people, the five minutes at the café counter is the only conversation of the day. Mastercard turns that overlooked ritual into a movement. Local merchants join as 'Regulars' places', and cardholders can opt in so the terminal greets them by the name they choose. A round-up Regulars Fund lets neighbours cover a fellow regular's usual order. The films never mention loneliness; they celebrate the barista who knows your order, the barber who notices a new haircut, the shopkeeper who asks about your mother. Nothing is tracked or flagged: recognition is human, mutual and opt-in. The message: some of the most valuable things in life happen at the checkout, and they are Priceless.

text_a: Known Here: The tap made paying effortless. It also made it anonymous. For many people, the checkout is the only conversation they have all day. Known Here puts a little of it back. text_a: On Me: Most lonely people aren't short of contacts. They're short of an easy first move. 'We should catch up' dies because reaching out feels like asking. On Me removes the ask. Send someone a pre-paid invitation to a specific place and time: 'Coffee at Rosa's, Thursday 4pm. On me.' They tap to accept, and Mastercard's sonic logo plays as a small 'hello'. After the meeting, they receive their own On Me to pass to someone else, so one invitation can start a chain of reunions. It never says 'lonely' and never sends cash, only a reason to show up. Launch in one city with independent cafés and a single issuer partner, then tell the stories of the chains. Priceless, made practical.
text_b: Tap Together: Convenience took away the small human moments of daily life. Mastercard gives them back with an invitation that can't be spent alone. Anyone can send a prepaid 'On Me' treat at a local café, barbershop, cinema or noodle bar, to a friend they've drifted from, a neighbour, a colleague or a relative. It unlocks only when both people tap their cards at the same terminal, so the tap becomes a gesture of showing up together. The sender takes the social risk, and the receiver is never labelled lonely. Local merchants gain footfall, and a loneliness charity partner helps with credibility and evaluation. Piloted in a few cities, it can grow through creators, community groups and gifting moments. The money starts it. The time together is priceless.
